newsitem.title: USA: U.S. traders, analysts doubt leak of Commerce data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. traders, analysts doubt leak of Commerce data.

text.p: Rumors of a leak in the July durable goods data on Friday were probably unfounded, most traders and analysts said.

On Friday, September Treasury bond futures fell almost from the start of trade and extended losses after the negative data, released 10 minutes after the open. Such a sharp move before data has stoked suspicions of a leak in the past.
While some Chicago Board of Trade bond traders growled about their leak suspicions on Friday and Monday, others said the talk was nothing but rumor-mongering.
At 0730 CDT/1230 GMT on Friday, the Commerce Department reported July that durable goods orders were up 1.6 percent, compared with an average Reuter poll forecast of a 0.3 percent gain.
Evelina Tainer, chief economist with IndoSuez Carr Futures, said Commerce Department leaks happened in the mid-1980s, but such breaches were much less likely today.
"They just really tightened up," Tainer said.
She noted that several forecasters had called for orders to rise 1.0 to 2.0 percent, with some estimates calling for a rise of as much as 4.0 percent.

"There certainly were as many forecasters predicting increases as decreases, so it was not all that unexpected," Tainer said. "It could have been one trader decided to take a bet on their economist. I think that's possible as opposed to thinking it was a leak."
In a market that is sometimes enamored with rumor and unmoved by fact, it is not so unusual for traders to subscribe to the leak theory, some said.
"Somebody's always going to say there's a leak if somebody moved before the number," said Donald Pullen, assistant vice president with Dean Witter Reynolds.
Others noted that trading by its very nature entails players making bets on economic data and the direction of the economy.
"People can be active before the number, but it doesn't really mean they have any more information," said Kurt Fraim, futures analyst with Aubrey G. Lanston.
But some floor brokers, who did not wish to be named, were not easily convinced that a breach had not occurred.
"This happens a lot and it really puts me behind the eight-ball," a bond options trader said on Friday.
"Anything is possible," said a notes futures trader.
"There is a lot of money out there and when there's that amount of money on the line you can't be sure about anything."
Others said hedge funds, thought to be among the big sellers on Friday, were merely squaring up their positions after two weeks of lethargic trade and before the weekend.
A Commerce Department official said there was no evidence of a durable goods leak.

"The Commerce Department takes seriously now as in the past its mission to protect the credibility of the data and prevent any breach of security," said Jane Callen, the Commerce official who conducts the "lock-ups" where the principal economic indicators are released.
--Chris Romans, Chicago Derivatives Desk (312) 408-8750
